passages.happening:
‘This is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth’ is the heading (verse 1).

‘O LORD, I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds. Revive them in these years; make them known in these years’ (verse 2). And then the prayer's great plea, “In Your wrath, remember mercy!” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
The heading and closing notes show that this prayer was meant to be sung. Shigionoth is an uncertain musical or literary term, linked to the heading of Psalm 7; it may mark a kind of lament or a style of performance. The note to the choirmaster with stringed instruments at the end matches the headings of many psalms and suggests the prayer was used in Israel's worship.

Verse 2 is the petition of the whole chapter. Habakkuk has heard what God did in the past, at the exodus and in the wilderness, and he asks God to do it again in his own years. He knows that judgment is coming. He does not ask God to cancel it. He asks God to remember mercy in the middle of it.
passages.later: Psalm 7's heading uses a related word, Shiggaion (Psalm 7:1). Moses had asked God to relent from his anger toward his people (Exodus 32:12).
passages.asks: Habakkuk asks God to remember mercy even in wrath. Ask what it would mean for you to pray that prayer for your own life, or for your city. And ask which of God's past deeds you most need him to do again.

passages.t: God comes from Teman to save
passages.happening:
‘God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran’ (verse 3). His glory covered the heavens, and his radiance was like the sun (verses 3-4). Plague went before him (verse 5). He stood and measured the earth, and the ancient mountains crumbled (verse 6). The tents of Cushan and Midian trembled (verse 7).

Was the LORD angry at the rivers and the sea, when he rode his chariots of salvation (verse 8)? The mountains quaked and the deep roared (verse 10). Sun and moon stood still at the flash of his arrows (verse 11). He marched across the earth in fury and threshed the nations (verse 12). ‘You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed’ (verse 13). He crushed the house of the wicked and trampled the sea with his horses (verses 13-15).
passages.hearers:
The chapter now describes God appearing, first speaking of him (verses 3-7), then speaking to him (verses 8-15). The poem draws on Israel's oldest memories. Teman was a region of Edom and Mount Paran lay in the wilderness south of Judah; both belong to the land Israel crossed after the exodus. Cushan and Midian were desert peoples of the same region.

The pictures of God as a warrior riding horses and chariots against rivers and sea drew on language Israel's neighbors used for their storm gods, who fought the sea and the forces of chaos. Israel's poets borrowed it to say that the LORD, not any other god, rules the waters. The parting of the sea and the crossing of the Jordan stand behind these lines, and the sun and moon standing still recall Joshua's battle.

The point of the poem is stated in verse 13. God goes out to save his people from their oppressors.
passages.later: At the Red Sea, ‘the LORD is a warrior’ (Exodus 15:3), and at Gibeon ‘the sun stood still and the moon stopped’ (Joshua 10:13). In his last words to Israel, Moses used the same picture: the LORD ‘shone forth from Mount Paran’ (Deuteronomy 33:2).
passages.hard:
Is the picture of God as a warrior who threshes the nations in anger compatible with the God of love?

The imagery of verses 8 to 15 comes from ancient warfare and storm poetry, and some readers find it troubling. Several things help. The poem's purpose is stated in verse 13: God goes out to save his people from oppressors. In the Bible's framework, God's anger is directed at evil that destroys, and the warrior fights for the helpless. The pictures are also heavily poetic, drawn from the memory of the exodus, and many of the details describe God's power over creation, rivers, sea and mountains, rather than human slaughter.

Some interpreters stress that the New Testament reinterprets the warrior picture, presenting Christ as conquering through the cross rather than the sword, while still looking toward a final judgment. Others stress continuity: the God who judges evil and the God who loves are the same, and a love indifferent to oppression would not be love. The poem gives no one a warrant to make war in God's name.
passages.asks: The poem says God goes out to save his people. Ask what you need saving from that you cannot fight yourself. And ask whether your picture of God has room for both his love and his anger at what destroys.

passages.t: Though the fig tree does not bud
passages.happening:
‘I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound’ (verse 16). Decay entered his bones. Yet he must wait quietly for the day of distress to come on the people who invade.

‘Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls’ (verse 17), “yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!” (verse 18). The Lord GOD is his strength, who makes his feet like a deer's and lets him walk on the heights (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Habakkuk trembles at what he has heard. The invasion he has been told of came on Judah in stages: the first deportation in 597 BC and the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. He resolves to wait for God's judgment on the invaders, which came when Persia took Babylon in 539 BC.

Verse 17 describes what an invasion meant for a farming people. Fig trees, vines, olive groves, fields, sheep and cattle were the whole economy, and armies stripped them bare. The verse lists six failures before the turn of verse 18, where he resolves to exult in the LORD. A deer's sure feet on the heights picture someone kept steady on dangerous ground.

The book that began with how long ends with the prophet's trust. Nothing has changed outside him yet. He has heard God, and that is enough to stand on.
passages.later: A psalm uses the same picture of sure feet: ‘He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights’ (Psalm 18:33).
passages.hard:
Does verse 18 mean a believer should feel joy when everything has failed?

Habakkuk does not pretend. He names every loss, and his body shakes with fear in verse 16. His joy in verse 18 is not a denial of grief or a mood he forces. It is a decision to hold on to God when nothing else holds. Many readers have found these verses a lifeline in hard seasons. They are not a rule that anyone in loss must feel happy, and they give no one a reason to tell a grieving person to rejoice.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Habakkuk lists everything that has failed, and still says God is his strength. Ask what you would put in that list in your own life now. And ask what it would mean to wait for God with trembling and trust together.
